findings.defect: The starburst is 14 ruler-straight hairlines of constant width running from the sun to the frame edges. Measured in flare-deep-space-ev12.png, the vertical spike has the same 3 px footprint at 60, 150 and 300 px from the sun (peak 229 over a 158 glow, 141 over 48, 75 over 0): no taper, no softening. The lines cross the night-side Earth in the limb view, and with the sun outside the frame (flare-sun-just-outside-frame-ev12.png) they still fan across the whole black picture. It reads at a glance as a vector asterisk drawn over the image, the stock lens-flare effect.
findings.realReference: In ISS, Shuttle and Apollo photographs with the sun in frame, the rays of a sunstar are wedges: as wide as the burned-out disc at the base, tapering to a point within a few degrees (roughly 2 to 6 diameters of the blown-out core), soft-edged, unequal in length, with a slight colour smear along the ray. They never appear as pixel-wide lines reaching the border, and a sun just outside the frame gives haze at that edge, not lines across the picture.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/flare.ts: STARBURST.spikeWidth = 0.0009 rad, a constant-angle Gaussian across the spike (FLARE_WGSL: across = theta * sin(dphi); gw = exp(-0.5 across^2 / w^2)). That is 0.56 px at 720p / 60 deg and five times narrower than the sun's own angular radius (0.0047 rad). A spike that thin is the diffraction pattern of a point source; the sun is a 0.53 deg disc and the pattern has to be convolved with it. The along profile is 1 / theta^2 normalised over the whole sphere with 45 % of the starburst energy (1 - FLARE_HALO_SHARE), so the thin line stays above the tonemap's black for hundreds of pixels.
findings.fixDirection: Convolve the spike set with the solar disc: across-profile half width = frame.sunDir.w (chord profile of a disc, or a Gaussian of about half the solar radius) in quadrature with the lens term. The same energy spread ten times wider lowers the peak tenfold, so each ray ends within a few degrees and shows as a tapered wedge whose visible length follows the exposure. Add per-blade irregularity (length and strength differing by 20-30 % per spike, fixed per blade) and keep the wavelength smear. Re-derive spikeIntegral and flareRadiance (CPU model) and add a display-image check: spike width at 60 px from the sun at least the disc diameter, no spike pixel above 3/255 beyond about 8 deg at EV 12-15, nothing but haze when the sun is off screen.

findings.defect: The ghosts are four perfect circles (ellipses off axis) on a straight line, flat-filled in pastel colours, each with the same concentric dark-red rim and an inner flat disc plus lighter annulus, like targets or stickers. They are bright, not faint: 173-234/255 at EV 12 (the third ghost is 223,231,234, nearly white), 163-178/255 over the night-side Earth in the limb view, and the 170 px green-grey one sits at 85-110/255 with an (80,69,19) rim.
findings.realReference: Real ghosts are images of the iris: polygons with the blade count (heptagons for this 7-blade lens, aligned with the rays), unevenly filled, mostly large and very dim, tinted by the coatings (green, magenta, amber at low saturation). Colour fringing is lateral, red on one side and blue on the other along the line through the image centre, not a ring all round. At an exposure for sunlit subjects they sit several stops under mid-grey and vanish over a lit Earth; many NASA frames with the sun in them show none.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/flare.ts GHOSTS: energies 6e-5 to 1.2e-4 of the sun's illuminance into radii of 0.016-0.08 rad. Example: 130,000 lx x 6e-5 / (pi x 0.016^2) is about 9,700 cd/m^2, twice mid-grey at EV 14.4; a coated two-reflection ghost is of order 2.5e-5 over 0.05 rad or more, about 400 cd/m^2. FLARE_WGSL ghost branch: disc = saturate((1 - r (1 +- shift)) / soft) scales each channel about the ghost's own centre (hence the concentric red rim), ring = disc x (0.55 + 0.45 smoothstep(0.6, 1, r)) makes the annulus; the profile is circular only.
findings.fixDirection: Aperture-shaped ghosts: a 7-sided mask at the rotation of the spike set, slightly curved edges, convolved with the solar disc so the edge is at least a solar radius soft. Chroma as a per-channel shift of the ghost centre along the axis-to-sun line (k per channel) instead of radial scaling. Uneven fill (gradient along that line, faint edge caustic). Cut the energies about 5-10 times and enlarge all but one, so no ghost exceeds roughly a quarter of mid-grey at the sunlit exposure; more, mostly sub-threshold ghosts of varied size rather than four equal-looking ones. Keep flareRadiance and the specs in step.

findings.defect: The glow round the sun is a neutral grey cone that ends at a definite radius. On a line between two spikes in the limb view the display value is 209 at 40 px, 129 at 80, 62 at 140, 27 at 180, 12 at 200, 2 at 220 and 0 from 240: it is still falling by 15 levels per 20 px when it hits black, so the eye sees the rim of a disc (plain in the 1440p view), with a khaki cast in the last 40 px. It looks like a soft halo sprite on black, which the requirement names as excluded ('halo sprites').
findings.realReference: Glare around the sun in orbital photography has no outer edge: a burned-out core, then a tail that keeps fading and merges into a haze over much of the frame (blacks near the sun are lifted, not zero), white to slightly warm, with no colour cast at its end.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/flare.ts HALO_POWER = 1.5, a pure theta^-3 law (core 0.012 rad, FLARE_HALO_SHARE 0.55 of 0.4 %), through the core's AgX encoding, which is about 30 display levels per stop down to a hard zero 12.5 stops under mid-grey: a theta^-3 tail loses its last 44 levels in 55 px. The hand-off records the finite radius (sections 3 and 7) as a property of the tonemap and leaves it. The core's bloom (4 %, linear) adds too little to hide it.
findings.fixDirection: Give the lens an ordinary glare spread function: add a theta^-2 skirt and a near-uniform veiling term (stray light, a fraction of a percent of the in-frame source spread over the field), normalised as now, so the display profile reaches its floor asymptotically. Ask core-support for an asymptotic black toe instead of the clip at the encoding's minimum. Check on the tonemapped image: radial profile monotonic, slope under about 0.2 levels per px where it meets its floor, R = G = B within 3 % along the tail.

findings.view: C:/dev/fable-space-game/out/screens/sky/orion-closeup-ev-5.png; crux-centaurus-ev-5.png; starfield-deep-space-ev-5.png; orientation-sirius.png; orientation-alnitak.png; orientation-acrux.png; leo-night-dark-adapted.png
findings.defect: Every star is the same hard little dot. In the Orion close-up Rigel and Betelgeuse (mag 0.1 and 0.5) clip to 18 px of area (under 5 px across), the belt stars to about 4 px across and sixth-magnitude stars to 2 px; 50 of the 61 clipped stars cover 4 px or less. Betelgeuse is a white core with a one-pixel orange rim. Orion cannot be picked out without working out where it should be (belt at the frame centre, Betelgeuse at 490,107, Rigel at 793,574); alpha and beta Centauri and the Southern Cross do not stand out in the Crux view either. The field reads as a random dot scatter.
findings.realReference: In a long exposure, and to the eye, a star's image grows steadily with its brightness because lens and eye point-spread functions have wide wings: first-magnitude stars are fat glowing discs with coloured halos several times the width of faint stars, so constellations are obvious at once. Betelgeuse is orange across its whole image, Rigel blue-white.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/shaders.ts STARS_WGSL and photometry.ts: one Gaussian of sigma 0.7 px (STAR_PSF_SIGMA_PX) in a fixed 6 x 6 px quad (STAR_QUAD_SIGMAS 4.3), capped by capAdditive(500). With no wings, six magnitudes of flux change the clipped radius by about 1.5 px, and a clipped core is white whatever the catalogue colour. The veiling-glare profile of the flare is applied to the sun only; the core's bloom is too weak to stand in for wings.
findings.fixDirection: One point-spread function with wings for every point source: Gaussian core plus a Moffat-type skirt (beta about 2-2.5, 10-20 % of the energy outside the core), normalised so the lattice sum still equals E / Omega_px. Size each star's quad from its pre-exposed flux (out to where the skirt drops under about 1/1024) so only the few hundred bright stars at the current exposure get large quads; the skirt carries the catalogue colour. Use the same profile for impostors. Keep the photometry spec (integrated flux within 5 %) and add a display check: visible diameter grows monotonically with flux and is at least three times larger at V 0 than at V 5 at EV -5.

findings.defect: At the exposure the game actually reaches in darkness (auto-exposure floor, EV100 -2.9) the night sky is a black frame with a few dozen dim dots: 99 % of the pixels are at 2/255 or below, 0.25 % above 8/255, and the Milky Way is at 1-5/255 (the hand-off's own figures: 2.1 at the galactic centre, 1.0 in Cygnus), which no display shows. The Magellanic Clouds appear only after multiplying the image by six. The good galactic-centre, Crux and Orion views are taken at a hand-set EV -5 that play cannot reach: EV_MIN is -3 and clamps the player's exposure compensation as well.
findings.realReference: From the night side of an orbit or from cislunar space the Milky Way is the main feature of the sky. ISS night photography (ISO 3200-12800, f/1.4-2.8, 0.5-2 s, about EV100 -4 to -7) shows a bright structured Milky Way and thousands of stars; Apollo crews in the Moon's shadow described a sky crowded with stars.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/core/post/exposure.ts: EV_DARK_FLOOR = -3 and EV_MIN = -3 (comment: 'stars and the Milky Way visible'). At that exposure 1e-3 cd/m^2 lies 4.7 stops under mid-grey, in the tonemap's toe. Core-owned; the sky criterion ('faintly visible') was passed at 2/255.
findings.fixDirection: Request to core-support: let the dark floor and EV_MIN go to about EV -6, reached by slow dark adaptation and only while nothing lit is metered. Then re-shoot leo-night-dark-adapted at the settled automatic exposure and assert display levels there (galactic centre at least about 25/255, Crux region about 40/255, well over a thousand stars above 16/255 in a 60 deg frame). This needs the star wings and the finer faint-star data of the other findings, because at EV -6 bright stars clip further and the cube's texels show.

findings.defect: Approaching a crescent Earth, the body changes brightness, colour and shape in jumps. At 0.5-4.2 px it is a bright blue-white round blob (peak 228,235,243 falling to 182,195,212). At 6.6 px it collapses to a two-pixel grey speck (peak 106,104,101; summed 8-bit luminance 13.5k against 50.2k one step earlier, with exposure already compensated for distance). At 13 and 21 px it returns as a dim neutral-grey crescent. The same mechanism reaches the Moon in the main mission: 0.52 deg is 3.5-5.6 px at 720 internal lines for 60-85 deg fields (the cockpit zooms 25-85 deg), so there the Moon is a round blob with no phase shape.
findings.realReference: In spacecraft imagery a shrinking Earth or Moon keeps its phase shape down to two or three pixels, and its total brightness and colour change smoothly (Earth stays blue-white, the Moon grey). Nothing fades out at an intermediate distance and comes back.
findings.likelyCause: (a) The core's TAA resolve keeps 25 % of the flux of a 1.4 px wide crescent (hand-off 6.1; docs/requests/sky-lighting-1.md still open; the same request covers the 7-10 % frame-to-frame variation of resolved stars). (b) Impostor flux is a Lambert sphere x geometricAlbedo coloured by meanColor / luma (feature.ts prepareImpostors, photometry.ts lambertSphereIlluminance), which matches neither the rendered body's phase curve nor its colour; the hand-off puts the Lambert Moon at several times the real one at quadrature. (c) The shape is a round Gaussian (impostorSigmaPx) cross-faded over only 3-6 px (IMPOSTOR_FULL_PX, IMPOSTOR_NONE_PX). (d) diameterPx uses frame.renderSize, the internal resolution, so dynamic resolution moves a body in and out of the impostor band.
findings.fixDirection: Make the impostor an analytic far level of detail instead of a blob: a lit sphere ray-cast inside the impostor quad (terminator from the body's sun direction, albedoLowRes or mean colour, coverage anti-aliased by the pixel footprint, convolved with the star profile). It carries the phase shape and does not depend on TAA. Hold it to about 12-16 px before handing over to geometry, where the resolve keeps 90 % or more. Take the phase curve and disc colour per body from data so flux and colour match the rendered body at the hand-over. Compute the size in display pixels, or add hysteresis, so resolution scaling cannot switch the representation. Assert on the tonemapped sheet: integrated flux within 15 % step to step and chromaticity within a small tolerance from 0.5 to 21 px.

findings.defect: At a 24 deg field (the cockpit zooms to 25 deg) the stars fainter than the catalogue come from the default 1024 cube as axis-aligned rectangular smudges 3-8 px across, blue and orange, between pin-sharp catalogue stars: visible texture magnification, and two different kinds of star in one picture. The 2048 cube in the same view looks like a real star field. It will show in play once the dark exposure is lowered.
findings.realReference: A telephoto star field has one kind of star at every brightness: round, sharper and more numerous towards the faint end, with no blocks.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/sky/feature.ts MILKY_WAY_FACE_SIZE = 1024 (0.088 deg per texel, 2.6 px at 24 deg / 720p) sampled bilinearly in BACKGROUND_FS; the catalogue stops at V 6.5 (8,920 stars), so V 6.5-10 stars live in the texture. Decision pending in docs/requests/sky-lighting-2.md. The two 1024-vs-2048 crop sheets are written by no spec and date from 2026-11-10.
findings.fixDirection: Either keep 2048 per face in a block-compressed HDR format (BC6H at 2048 costs about what rgb9e5 costs at 1024), or better, move the stars down to about V 9-10 into the instanced catalogue (background pass measured at 0.013 ms of its 0.08 ms budget) and leave only unresolved glow in the cube. At the least use a bicubic or Gaussian magnification filter so texels are not rectangles.

findings.defect: The Milky Way changes hue with exposure and turns rust-brown as it dims: at EV -3 the bright part of the bulge is (26,15,11), R/G 1.7 and R/B 2.4-3.0, where at EV -5 the bulge is a warm grey (62,51,47), R/G 1.2 and R/B 1.3.
findings.realReference: A dim Milky Way is colourless silver-grey to the dark-adapted eye and neutral to warm white in an underexposed photograph. It does not go red when it gets fainter.
findings.likelyCause: The per-channel toe of the core's AgX tonemap (the weaker channels reach black first) acting on the warm colour of the SVS map. Not in the sky code.
findings.fixDirection: Request to core-support: treat the toe on luminance, or desaturate towards neutral at very low levels (night vision is colourless), then re-shoot. Lowering the dark floor moves the band out of the toe and removes most of it.

findings.defect: The views that should show the probe and the limb sun are staged on the lab planet (flat green and blue map, blocky cloud shell, no atmosphere), so none can be held against a photograph, and two do not show what the hand-off says. In pbr-spheres-leo-day the shadowed, Earth-facing parts of the white and grey spheres are at 10/255 and 1-2/255 beside a cloud deck at 150/255 (hand-off: 'Earth-facing halves lit by the cloudy Earth'). pbr-spheres-leo-night is a black frame (99th percentile 1/255) with four specular dots; the spheres cannot be seen. The limb view has no atmosphere arc, so the orbital sunrise with flare has not been looked at.
findings.realReference: Earth-facing white surfaces of a spacecraft in daylight orbit are a clear blue-tinted light grey, roughly a fifth of the sunlit side. Orbital sunrise is the sun breaking through a thin blue-to-orange arc of atmosphere.
findings.likelyCause: labs/sky stand-ins (LabPlanet, the clouds=1 shell): the lab ocean under the vessel has an albedo near 0.03 and there is no atmosphere; integration with atmosphere-clouds was not run by the package (hand-off section 7). In the integration lab the probe does light the vehicle's Earth side plausibly (out/screens/integration/budget-leo.png), so this is missing evidence, not a probe fault. Screenshots were regenerated 2026-11-11 07:51-07:53 (23 of 23 functional specs passed); perf-1440p-leo-horizon.png comes from the perf project and is from 2026-11-10.
findings.fixDirection: Add integration-lab views for this package's main shots and judge those: the sun 5-7 deg above the limb with the real atmosphere and the flare; the sphere set or the vehicle over a cloud field in daylight orbit, with a check that a white surface facing the Earth is 0.15-0.25 of the sunlit side; low orbit at night at the automatic exposure. In the sky lab, at least place the vessel over cloud.

findings.defect: No emission nebulae appear. In the 24 deg Orion view the sword (around 635,500) is a few dots with no Orion Nebula; the Carina region has no glow either.
findings.realReference: In a long exposure of this field the Orion Nebula is the most conspicuous object after the bright stars: a pink-white glow about a degree across (30 px here), visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy star. The Carina Nebula is similar in the southern Milky Way.
findings.likelyCause: The cube is built from NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020 (star catalogues and a Gaia-derived Milky Way layer), which carry starlight and dust but appear to carry no nebular emission (docs/handoff/bake-moon-sky.md). Data owned by the sky bake, not by this package.
findings.fixDirection: Request to the sky bake: composite a handful of bright extended objects (Orion Nebula, Carina, Lagoon, Andromeda) from a freely licensed photographic all-sky panorama into the cube, scaled to literature surface brightness.
